prime.problem: Locks fix races, but a thread that holds one lock while waiting for another can end up in a cycle: T1 holds A and wants B, T2 holds B and wants A. Nothing crashes and nothing is logged; the program just stops. You need to know exactly what makes that possible, so you can make it impossible.
prime.fits: First card of Concurrency issues. It is the cost of the Synchronization part: every lock from locks, mutexes, semaphores and monitors can take part in a cycle. Livelock (next) is what the obvious timeout-and-retry fix can turn into.
expect: the wait-for graph and its cycle
prime.goal: Spot a deadlock from code or a wait-for graph, name the condition each fix breaks, and prove why a global lock order can't form a cycle.

attend: What does the barrier in the demo force, and why would the deadlock appear only sometimes without it?
Which of the four conditions does acquire(timeout=1) break, and which does ordered() break?
Why does ranking every lock and acquiring in increasing rank make a cycle impossible, and not just unlikely?
In the philosophers' fix, why does changing only P4's order break the cycle for all five?
When can you not impose a global order, and what do databases do instead?

must: Deadlock needs all four at once: mutual exclusion + hold and wait + no preemption + circular wait → remove any one → it can't happen → each fix is a choice of which condition to break

Give every lock a rank and always acquire in increasing rank → every "waits on" arrow points to a higher rank → a cycle would need a lock ranked below itself → circular wait is impossible, at no runtime cost (0.0019 s, all 5 philosophers ate)
Time out and back off breaks no-preemption (the holder gives up its own lock) → progress resumes, but only after the timeout (1.00 s of nothing) → and threads that retry in step can livelock

One instance per lock → a cycle in the wait-for graph is exactly a deadlock → detection walks "waits on" arrows until one repeats (['T1', 'T2', 'T1']) → databases detect and abort a victim, because transactions can roll back
elevated: The demo sorts locks by id() to get a global order → any total order works as long as every code path uses the same one → the cost is discipline, not CPU
reference: Coffman et al. 1971 and OSTEP chapter 32
threading.Barrier and the exact philosopher run counts (2, 1, 4, 3, 3, 4)

compress.prompt: From memory, list the four conditions, and beside each write the fix that breaks it and what that fix costs. Then write the three-line argument for why a global lock order can't form a cycle.
checklist: hold and wait → take all locks at once (less concurrency)
no preemption → timeout and back off (wasted time, livelock risk)
every wait points up in rank, so no path returns to where it started
a cycle in the wait-for graph = deadlock, with one instance per resource

retrieve.q: Explain why deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions, using the A/B example to show each one.
answer: mutual exclusion: A and B are Locks, one owner each
hold and wait: each thread keeps its first lock inside with first: while asking for the second
no preemption: T2 can't take A from T1
circular wait: T1 → T2 → T1; remove any one and the standoff can't form

retrieve.q: Walk through the demo run with the barrier, from t = 0 to the end, and explain why T2 finishes but T1 doesn't get both.
answer: both take their first lock, then meet at the barrier, so each holds one
both call acquire(second, timeout=1) and wait on each other
at 1.00 s one of them (here T1) times out, leaves its with and releases its lock
the other now gets its second lock: "got both"; which thread times out varies by run

retrieve.q: You own a service where each request locks two of 1,000 accounts. Compare one big lock, a global order and detect-and-abort for it, with the cost of each.
answer: one big lock: no deadlock, but all requests serialise even on unrelated accounts
global order (e.g. by account id): no deadlock, full concurrency, costs discipline on every code path
detect-and-abort: needs the ability to roll back half-done work; natural in a database, awkward in plain threads

compare.q: Deadlock vs livelock: what is each thread doing, which design choice turns a deadlock fix into a livelock, and how do you tell them apart on a running system?
answer: deadlock: all blocked, CPU near zero; livelock: all running, retrying, CPU busy
the timeout-and-release fix breaks no-preemption, but identical threads with identical waits retry in lockstep
tell them apart by CPU use and by whether state keeps changing; fix livelock with random backoff or, better, a lock order

compare.q: Finding a deadlock is finding a cycle in the wait-for graph; toposort fails exactly when a graph has a cycle. What does a global lock order correspond to in toposort terms?
answer: a global rank is a topological order imposed in advance on all locks
acquiring in increasing rank means every wait edge goes forward in that order, so the graph stays acyclic (a DAG)
detection is the reverse: run a cycle search (like toposort's leftover nodes or DFS back-edges) on the current wait-for graph

predict.q: Three threads: T1 takes A then B, T2 takes B then C, T3 takes C then A, all forced to collide with a barrier and acquire(timeout=1) on the second lock. Is there a deadlock, what does the wait-for graph look like, and how many threads get both locks? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Yes: T1 → T2 → T3 → T1 is a 3-cycle. After 1 s at least one thread times out and releases its first lock, which lets the thread waiting on it finish; how many finish depends on who times out first and when, just as the card's philosophers ate 1 to 4 across runs. Sorting each pair by a global order breaks it: T3 would take A before C, so no cycle can close.

apply.task: Extend code/deadlock.py with the three-thread cycle (A→B, B→C, C→A). Run it forced with a barrier, and print the wait-for graph just before the timeouts using the file's find_cycle. Then fix it with ordered() and time the fixed run. Finally, write the cycle for 5 philosophers and mark which single thread's order you'd change.
apply.done: The forced run shows a 3-cycle (for example ['T1', 'T2', 'T3', 'T1']) and at least one timeout after about 1 s; the ordered run finishes in milliseconds with all three getting both locks; your philosopher answer changes only the thread whose two forks wrap around (P4: f0 before f4).
apply.hint: With one instance per lock, the wait-for graph is just thread → holder of the lock it's waiting for. Build it as a dict before calling acquire, since you can't inspect it after the timeout.
